# Background & Rationale

An estimated 85% of health research resources are wasted globally due to poorly prioritized questions, weak design, non-publication, and poor reporting. In LMICs, physician-scientists face structural, logistical, and career barriers that limit valid, high-value research.

Egyptian and regional studies report top barriers: lack of funding, time, lab access, research skills/training, poor collaboration, and low institutional attention; supervision quality is frequently implicated but less quantified. Reducing waste requires identifying barriers and aligning priorities, methods, supervision, and incentives.

# Research question

Which barriers most strongly limit the ability of early-career researchers to conduct valid, relevant, and non-wasteful research, and which interventions should be prioritized to address them?

# Objectives

- Identify the principal barriers affecting early-career medical research in Egypt.

- Reach consensus on the relative importance and modifiability of each barrier.

- Reach consensus on priority interventions to improve research validity and reduce waste.

- Identify which interventions are feasible at the individual, supervisory, institutional, and national levels.

- Produce a prioritized action framework for Egyptian medical schools, hospitals, research offices, funders, and policymakers.

# Key Definition

**Early-career medical researcher:** Medical students, house officers, residents, teaching assistants, and assistant lecturers in Egyptian medical schools, teaching hospitals, and research institutions.

# Study Design

This study will use a two-round modified Delphi consensus design. The Delphi panel will include early-career medical researchers, supervisors, research methodologists, research administrators, funders, policymakers, and other stakeholders with relevant experience in Egyptian medical research. The process will identify barriers, assess their importance and modifiability, and prioritize feasible interventions to improve research validity and reduce waste.

# Setting & Population

- **Setting:** Multiple Egyptian medical schools and affiliated teaching hospitals across regions (Greater Cairo, Delta and Alexandria, Upper Egypt).
- **Participants:**
  - Early-career researchers (as defined).
  - Supervisors (professors, associate professors, and lecturers actively supervising research).
  - Ethics committee members.
  - Funders, policymakers, or research administrators.
  - Health-system representatives.

# Sampling

A purposive, maximum-variation sample of approximately 80–100 panelists will be invited. The study will seek representation across career stage, discipline, institution type, geographic region, research experience, and stakeholder role. The target is at least 60 completed responses in Round 1 and 50–60 completed responses in Round 2.

Panel composition

- Early-career researchers 35
- Research supervisors 25
- Biostatisticians and methodologists 15
- Ethics committee members 5
- Funders, policymakers, or research administrators 10
- Health-system representatives 5

# Data Collection

Round 1 will consist of a structured questionnaire containing evidence-informed barrier statements, importance and modifiability ratings, and open-ended questions. Round 2 will present retained items with anonymized group feedback and ask participants to re-rate them and assess proposed interventions for importance and feasibility. The same panelists will be invited to both rounds using individual anonymous identifiers.

# Data Analysis

Analysis will include median, interquartile range, percentage agreement, and response distributions for each item in each round. Consensus will be predefined as at least 75% rating an item 7–9 with a median of at least 7 and IQR no greater than 2. Intervention priority will additionally require at least 70% agreement on feasibility. Changes between rounds, item retention, attrition, and subgroup variation will be reported transparently in accordance with CREDES recommendations.

# Outcomes

## Primary outcome

The ranked list of barriers that reach consensus as important contributors to invalid or low-value medical research among early-career researchers in Egypt.

## Secondary outcomes

- Barriers reaching consensus as highly modifiable.

- Interventions reaching consensus as high-priority and feasible.

- Differences in ratings between stakeholder groups.

- Change in median ratings and agreement between Rounds 1 and 2.

- Areas of persistent disagreement.

- Final intervention framework organized by level:

  - Individual.

  - Supervisor.

  - Department or institution.

  - National policy or funding system

# Bias Considerations

- **Selection bias:** Multi-institution sampling; weighting; compare respondents vs non-respondents.

# Ethics & Governance

This study will be conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and applicable Egyptian regulations governing research involving human participants. Ethical approval will be sought from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at Faculty of Medicine, MTI University, and, where required, from participating institutions. Because the study involves human participants completing questionnaires, informed consent will be obtained electronically at the beginning of each Delphi round. The consent form will describe the study purpose, procedures, potential risks and benefits, voluntary nature of participation, right to withdraw at any time without penalty, data protection measures, and contact information for the research team and ethics committee. Participation will be entirely voluntary, and no financial or academic incentives that could be perceived as coercive will be offered.

All data will be de-identified at the point of collection. Each participant will be assigned a unique anonymous identifier that will be used to link responses across rounds without revealing their identity. Names, email addresses, and other direct identifiers will be stored separately from survey responses in password-protected, access-controlled files on secure institutional servers. Only the core research team will have access to identifiable contact information, which will be used solely for study coordination (sending Round 2 invitations) and will be deleted after the study is completed and the data are archived. Qualitative comments will be anonymized during analysis; any potentially identifying information will be removed or generalized before reporting.

Data will be retained for seven years after study completion in accordance with institutional policy and then securely destroyed. Findings will be reported in aggregate form; no individual participant will be identifiable in publications, presentations, or policy briefs. Because the Delphi method relies on expert opinion rather than clinical interventions or sensitive personal data, the study is anticipated to pose minimal risk to participants. The main potential risks include discomfort when rating sensitive topics and concerns about confidentiality. These risks will be mitigated by emphasizing anonymity, using neutral and non-judgmental wording, allowing participants to skip any item, and providing contact information for the research team should participants have questions or concerns. If any participant expresses distress or raises concerns about specific institutional practices, the research team will respond appropriately and, where necessary, refer the matter to relevant institutional authorities while maintaining participant confidentiality.

Given that the panel may include individuals in supervisory or leadership positions, additional care will be taken to prevent perceived coercion. Junior participants (medical students, residents, early-career researchers) will be explicitly assured that their participation or non-participation will not affect their academic standing, supervision, or career progression. Invitations will be sent directly to potential participants rather than through supervisors or department heads wherever possible. The study protocol, consent forms, and all participant-facing materials will be reviewed and approved by the ethics committee before any data collection begins. Any substantial protocol amendments will be submitted for ethical review and approval prior to implementation.
